questions.stem: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a plant shoot. A student sets up a potometer and measures how far an air bubble moves in 5 minutes. Why does the potometer measure water UPTAKE rather than transpiration directly?

options.text: Transpiration is too difficult to see
Not all water taken up is lost through transpiration -- some is used in photosynthesis and other processes, but water uptake closely approximates transpiration rate
The potometer blocks transpiration from occurring
Water uptake and transpiration are always exactly equal

questions.explanation: The potometer tracks how quickly water moves into the shoot by measuring air bubble movement. While most water absorbed (about 99%) is indeed lost through transpiration, a small amount is used in photosynthesis and to maintain cell turgidity. So the potometer gives a close estimate of transpiration rate, but not an exact measurement.

questions.stem: When setting up a potometer, the shoot must be cut underwater. Why is this step critical?

options.text: To prevent the shoot from drying out
To prevent air bubbles entering the xylem, which would break the continuous water column and stop water movement
To clean the cut surface of bacteria
To allow the shoot to absorb water faster

questions.explanation: If the shoot is cut in air, air can enter the xylem vessels and form air locks. These air bubbles break the continuous column of water in the xylem, preventing the transpiration pull from working. Cutting underwater ensures water (not air) enters the cut xylem vessels, maintaining the continuous water column needed for transpiration.

questions.stem: A student uses a potometer to compare transpiration rates under different conditions. In which condition would the air bubble move fastest?

options.text: Still air at room temperature
A fan blowing on the leaves at room temperature
Leaves covered in petroleum jelly (vaseline) at room temperature
In a sealed plastic bag at room temperature

questions.explanation: A fan increases air movement around the leaves, removing the layer of humid air (boundary layer) that builds up near the stomata. This maintains a steep diffusion gradient, increasing the rate of transpiration and therefore water uptake. The bubble would move fastest in this condition. Vaseline blocks stomata, and a plastic bag traps humidity -- both reduce transpiration.

questions.stem: A student's potometer results are inconsistent -- the air bubble sometimes moves backwards. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The plant is photosynthesising
There is a leak in the apparatus, allowing air or water in at connections
The plant has too many leaves
The temperature is too high

questions.explanation: Leaks in the potometer apparatus are the most common cause of unreliable results. Air entering through loose connections can form additional bubbles or cause the tracking bubble to move erratically. All joints must be sealed with waterproof grease, and the apparatus must be checked for airtightness before starting.

questions.stem: To reset the potometer for repeated readings, the student opens the reservoir tap to push the air bubble back to the starting position. Why is it important to take multiple readings?

options.text: To use up all the water in the reservoir
To calculate a mean, which increases the reliability of the results and helps identify anomalies
To give the plant time to adjust
Multiple readings are not necessary if the first one is accurate

questions.explanation: Repeating measurements and calculating a mean (average) increases reliability by reducing the effect of random errors and anomalous results. Biological experiments often have natural variation, so a single reading may not be representative. Taking at least three repeats allows identification and exclusion of outliers, giving a more trustworthy average.
